description_full: Teledyne Technologies Incorporated provides enabling technologies for industrial growth markets in the United States, Europe, Asia, and internationally. The Digital Imaging segment provides visible spectrum sensors and digital cameras; and infrared, ultraviolet, visible, and X-ray spectrum products, as well as micro-electromechanical systems and semiconductors, such as analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converters. This segment offers cooled and uncooled infrared or thermal products, including sensors, camera cores, and camera systems; high-resolution, low-dose X-ray sensors, high-power microwave, and high-energy X-ray subsystems; and instruments for the measurement of physical properties and maritime products, as well as develops and manufactures multi-spectrum electro-optic/infrared imaging systems and associated products, such as lasers, optics, radars, CBRNE (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and explosive) detectors, and unmanned air and ground systems. The Instrumentation segment provides monitoring, control, and electronic test and measurement equipment; and power and communications connectivity devices for distributed instrumentation systems and sensor networks. The Aerospace and Defense Electronics segment offers electronic and optical components and subsystems, data acquisition and communications components and equipment, harsh-environment interconnects, general aviation batteries and other components; and onboard avionics systems and ground-based applications, aircraft data and connectivity solutions, hardware systems, and software applications. The Engineered Systems segment provides systems engineering, integration and advanced technology development, and complex manufacturing solutions for defense, space, environmental, and energy applications; and designs and manufactures electrochemical energy systems and specialty electronics for military applications. The company was founded in 1960 and is headquartered in Thousand Oaks, California.

financial_summary: Teledyne Technologies Incorpora is a large-cap technology business with a $29.7B market cap on $6.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.33× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 19× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 1.4%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 19% operating margin runs 12pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+2.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 536 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 31% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.89, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $181.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 49% in the 2020 crash, 32% in the 2022 bear market and 66% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $569 (margin of safety -13%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 28%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $249 to $1,265 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 14% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $770 on average, 19% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 11.1% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.6%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.22).
It converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.33x.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 5.2% of revenue on R&D.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.4x net debt to EBITDA ($352.4M of cash against $2.5B of debt), with interest covered 19.3x.
Goodwill makes up 57% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.9% over 3 years, 14.7% over 5 years and 10.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 34%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.15 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 75% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 18%.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (1.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 7.9% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.8%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (13 sales, net $14.9M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.4% (1.4% in buybacks).
people: With about 15,800 employees, each generates about $387K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and revenue has grown 9.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $68K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.9M (5x revenue per employee).
